title: Smaller Values to the Right
statement:
You get an integer array nums. For every index i, count how many elements to its right are strictly smaller than nums[i], that is, the number of j > i with nums[j] < nums[i].

Return the counts as an array of the same length as nums.

examples.why: For the first 7, the values to its right are 1, 7, 2. The other 7 is equal, not smaller, so only 1 and 2 count.
Strictly decreasing: everything to the right of an element is smaller.

hints: Process the array from right to left. Then 'elements to my right' becomes 'elements I have already seen'.
You need a structure that stores the seen values and answers 'how many are smaller than x?' quickly. A sorted list with binary search answers it, but inserting into it costs O(n).

Values lie in a small range, so shift them to 1…20 001 and use a Fenwick (binary indexed) tree of counts: query the prefix below x, then add 1 at x. Merge sort that counts how many right-half elements jump ahead of each left element also works.

explain.intuition:
Scan from the right. When you reach index i, everything to its right has already been seen, so the question becomes: how many of the values seen so far are smaller than nums[i]? That is a "count in a prefix of values" query mixed with inserts.

A Fenwick tree does both in O(log V). Index it by value (shifted so the smallest value is 1) and store how many times each value has been seen. The prefix sum up to nums[i] − 1 is the answer for i; then add one at nums[i]. Using nums[i] − 1, not nums[i], is what keeps equal values out.
steps: Shift values: v = nums[i] + 10 001, so they lie in 1 … 20 001. Create a Fenwick array of that size, all zeros.
For i from n − 1 down to 0: set result[i] = prefix(v − 1).
Then add(v, 1) so later (more left) indexes see this value.
prefix(x) sums tree[x] while stripping the lowest set bit of x; add(x) adds while adding the lowest set bit.
pitfalls: Counting equal values by querying prefix(v) instead of prefix(v − 1).
Scanning left to right, which counts elements on the wrong side.
Forgetting to shift negative values before using them as Fenwick indexes; index 0 makes the update loop never end.

solutions.title: Check every pair
solutions.idea: For each index, scan everything to its right and count the smaller values.

solutions.title: Fenwick tree over values, right to left
solutions.idea: Walk from the right. Ask the Fenwick tree how many seen values are below the current one, then record the current value.

solutions.title: Merge sort that counts jumps
solutions.idea: Sort indexes by value with merge sort. When a left-half element is placed, every right-half element already placed before it is smaller and was to its right.

followups: Values range up to 10⁹ instead of 10 000. What do you do before building the Fenwick tree?
Count, for each index, the elements to its right that are more than twice as large. Which of the two fast methods adapts more easily?
